doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Teaching improvisation to young students with two notes
summary: Children are innately creative; Mondello eases fear by giving a student two notes and building up without theory.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Very, very good point. I see that and have seen that in my years teaching. I’ve always felt that younger students have an innate creative ability to, what we would call improvise, in many different ways. You see that in art work, you see that in their speaking. The thing about offering jazz improv “quote quote” to let’s say a fifth or sixth grader, okay, is — it can be as you say very, very intimidating. Students, and you know this, at that age, you know, they don’t want to be ridiculed and they don’t want to be heckled. However, once you can ease that hesitation, and there are ways to do that that you kind of learn over the years okay? Now you’re not going to have a sixth grade kid, you know, improvising like John Coltrane, okay, unless your name is Clovis Grognuz over in Switzerland. I don’t know if you’ve ever seen him.

Oh you’ve got to check him out. I mean this kid, and I had an opportunity to profile him. He literally — he’s a savant and he’s learned Bird solos, Coltrane solos, Dexter Gordon solos. Note for note. And he’s done it this way. He doesn’t follow the process of looking at a transcription, playing the notes and then you know, he goes the other way, which is of course the way a lot of older players have learned you know. But I’ll tell you, as an educator, one little trick that I’ve used with a lot of success — and the thing about it is that once the kids do that, “Hey man look at me, this is pretty cool, I just played along with — you know you put on an Aebersold or you know some YouTube downloaded backing track. Maybe it’s just like a rock guitar with a rhythm section, and you give the kid two notes, a G and an F. Okay? On the horn. And then you know I pick up the horn, you play those two notes, the kid plays it. No music. Then you embellish the two notes

and then that two notes becomes a little more involved rhythmically and you try to keep it within the technical abilities of the student, which is of course the teacher’s responsibility, and then you tell the student, “You know what you have done? You have just played jazz. You have just improvised, okay?” And then you — and again this is things that have worked. I mean there are things that I’ve done that just fell flat as a flat tire okay. But you want to get the child or the student feeling confident about having done something in a very small way.

And then it just goes on and on and on from there. And when you get the “I don’t know what to play” comment, okay, well try to play what I’m going to play for you. And then of course from the two notes to the three notes to maybe a version of a scale, don’t get into any theoretical circle of fifths or anything like that, because then you wind up with the intimidation, and oh my God it’s like the Periodic Table of the Elements. “I can’t handle that.”
